entry.title: Inside FFmpeg: A Source Tour of the Demux, Decode, Filter, Encode and Mux Threads

link.title: Inside FFmpeg: A Source Tour of the Demux, Decode, Filter, Encode and Mux Threads

entry.content:
Run ffmpeg -i fourk.mov -c:v libx264 -crf 23 out.mp4 on a long 4K clip and the machine hums for an hour. The only visible feedback is that one line ticking upward: frame= 48211 fps= 41 q=23.0 size= .... It looks like a single loop. It is not. Inside the process, compressed packets, raw frames and encoded packets are being pushed through several queues between threads that start, block and finish independently of each other.

The interesting part is what happens to one single frame. It gets read off disk as a compressed packet, handed to a decoder thread, pulled out as raw pixels, pushed into a filter graph — your -vf scale=1920:1080 lives there — dragged back out, fed into the encoder, and finally interleaved into the output container by yet another thread. None of these stages sit in a straight line inside one function; they coordinate through a scheduler in fftools/ffmpeg_sched.c.

This tour follows that flow through the current master sources, and every claim links to a specific line on GitHub so you can click through and argue with it. If you enjoy watching real codebases from the inside, our earlier looks at the SDL window-and-events core, the LÖVE2D Lua runtime, and Godot engine internals make good companion reading.

The whole transcode flow on master: main() and transcode() orchestrate, the scheduler gives every stage its own thread, and data moves demux → decode → filter → encode → mux through scheduler queues. Each node maps to a real file in the repository.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main() is a dispatcher, not a worker. main, L995 allocates the scheduler, parses options and hands off to transcode() — the whole file is only about 1,070 lines long.
  • transcode() owns the main loop. transcode, L901 starts every worker with sch_start(), then loops on sch_wait(), printing the famous frame= fps= q= line via print_report().
  • The scheduler turns each stage into a thread. task_start, L414 calls pthread_create() once per demuxer, decoder, filter graph, encoder and muxer task.
  • The demuxer thread reads the input. input_thread, L843 loops on av_read_frame() and routes each packet through demux_send(), applying bitstream filters on the way.
  • libavformat does the container parsing. av_read_frame, L1646 funnels down to ff_read_packet(), where MOV, MKV and TS plug in their own per-container callbacks.
  • Decoding is push-then-pull. decoder_thread, L909 blocks on sch_dec_receive() for the next packet, then packet_decode() calls avcodec_send_packet() and pulls decoded frames back out.
  • The filter graph runs in its own thread. filter_thread, L3507 receives frames, lazily builds and configures the graph, feeds it via buffersrc and drains buffersink toward the encoder.
  • The muxer thread interleaves and writes. muxer_thread, L401 keeps streams in sync through a SyncQueue and writes through av_interleaved_write_frame().

The detail view: 34 functions across seven groups, following one frame from ff_read_packet() all the way to av_interleaved_write_frame(), including every queue crossing between threads.

One process, several threads

The scheduler is the spine. sch_alloc() (ffmpeg_sched.c, L625) sets up a table of task nodes; the node kinds are enumerated in fftools/ffmpeg_sched.h as SCH_NODE_TYPE_DEMUX through SCH_NODE_TYPE_FILTER_OUT (L93). sch_start() (L1767) walks the table and calls task_start() on each node — that is where pthread_create() happens (L425). From this point the main thread stops doing media work: transcode() just waits on sch_wait() (L1833), handles keyboard interaction and prints periodic reports.

What crosses between threads? Packets and frames, through queues owned by the scheduler: sch_dec_send() (L2419) publishes decoded frames to whichever filter graph consumes them, sch_filter_receive() (L2581) is the blocking pull on the filter side, sch_filter_send() (L2659) hands filtered frames to the encoder, and sch_enc_send() (L2532) routes compressed packets toward the muxer. Registration happens long before any thread starts: ifile_open() (ffmpeg_demux.c, L2318) calls sch_add_demux() with input_thread as the function pointer. Bitstream filters run on the demuxer side too, before a packet is queued: demux_send() pushes each one through the bsf chain built by do_bsf_graph() (L615), so something like an annex-B conversion never blocks a decode thread. That design explains what you see in htop during a transcode: no thread does everything, and each one spends much of its life blocked on a queue.

The queues themselves are shallow on purpose. queue_alloc() (L382) builds them on top of fftools/thread_queue.c, and the default depths are tiny: DEFAULT_PACKET_THREAD_QUEUE_SIZE is 2 (ffmpeg_sched.h, L257) and DEFAULT_FRAME_THREAD_QUEUE_SIZE is 2 (L262). A slow filter thread therefore applies backpressure all the way to the demuxer instead of letting the process balloon in memory — one reason ffmpeg transcodes hour-long files without eating your RAM.

Packet in, frame out: the decode loop

decoder_thread() (ffmpeg_dec.c, L909) is a tight loop: block on sch_dec_receive() (L924), then call packet_decode() (L950). packet_decode() pushes the packet in with avcodec_send_packet() (L719) and loops on avcodec_receive_frame_flags() (L749) until the codec has nothing more to give. Inside libavcodec, avcodec_send_packet() (decode.c, L738) buffers the packet and decode_receive_frame_internal() (L669) drives decode_simple_receive_frame() (L617) until a frame pops out.

One drift worth knowing: on current master, avcodec_receive_frame() itself no longer lives in decode.c — it is defined in libavcodec/avcodec.c, L718. If your local tree is older, look in decode.c; if newer, look in avcodec.c. Decoded frames leave through sch_dec_send() (called at L820), which wakes the filtergraph thread. That is the entire decode stage: packets in, frames out, one dedicated thread per decoder.

The filtergraph thread

filter_thread() (L3507) does three jobs. First it lazily builds the graph: the first frame triggers configure_filtergraph() (called at L3523, defined at L2187), which allocates an AVFilterGraph, inserts a buffersrc per graph input and a buffersink per output (L1751 for video, L1882 for audio), then calls avfilter_graph_config() (L2268) to negotiate pixel and sample formats. Second it feeds frames: send_frame() (L3242, called from the loop at L3575) pushes into buffersrc. Third it drains: read_frames() pulls results via av_buffersink_get_frame_flags() (L2934) and hands each one to sch_filter_send() (L2891).

Underneath, libavfilter does the real work. avfilter_graph_config() (avfiltergraph.c, L1480) runs the negotiation; after that, each push into buffersrc triggers ff_filter_graph_run_once() (L1675, reached from buffersrc.c, L212), which advances one activation — and filter_frame_to_filter() (avfilter.c, L1202) is where your filter’s code finally executes. Every -vf option you have ever typed is processed here, one frame at a time.

Encode, sync, mux

The encoder mirrors the decoder. encoder_thread() (ffmpeg_enc.c, L998) blocks on sch_enc_receive() (L1026) for the next frame, and frame_encode() (L867) drives encode_frame() (L683), which calls avcodec_send_frame() (L722) and loops on avcodec_receive_packet() (L734). Encoded packets leave via sch_enc_send() (L529) toward the muxer thread. Subtitle encoders open immediately (L1019); audio and video encoders open lazily on their first frame through enc_open() (L413), triggered by a scheduler callback.

The muxer thread (muxer_thread(), L401) pulls packets with sch_mux_receive() (L420) and keeps streams interleaved through sync_queue_process() (L244): sq_send() at L249, sq_receive() at L258 — the SyncQueue API itself lives in fftools/sync_queue.c (L343, L596). Writing goes through write_packet() → av_interleaved_write_frame() (L230); libavformat’s own av_interleaved_write_frame, L1268 reorders packets by DTS. The container header is written by avformat_write_header, L512 once every stream is ready, and of_write_trailer() (L785) closes things out after sch_stop(). If you pass -c copy, most of this tour is skipped: of_streamcopy() (L454) routes packets demux → mux directly.

From configure script to ffmpeg.exe

Some real build facts from the master tree, observed while preparing this tour:

  • The build starts with configure, an 8,883-line shell script that probes your toolchain, libraries and CPU features before generating config.mak.
  • Hand-written x86 assembly defaults to nasm (x86asmexe_default="nasm", configure, L4415). If it is missing, the script dies with “nasm not found or too old. Please install/update nasm or use –disable-x86asm” (L6757) — and that flag quietly removes most SIMD speedups, which is why nobody ships it in release builds.
  • The binary is assembled from the split modules: fftools/Makefile lists ffmpeg_dec.o, ffmpeg_demux.o, ffmpeg_enc.o, ffmpeg_filter.o, ffmpeg_hw.o, ffmpeg_mux.o, ffmpeg_mux_init.o, ffmpeg_opt.o, ffmpeg_sched.o, sync_queue.o and thread_queue.o as objects for the ffmpeg target. The thread split you saw in the diagrams is visible right in the build file.
  • ffplay builds beside it and is the reason SDL shows up in the dependency graph: configure line 4369 sets ffplay_deps="avcodec avformat avfilter swscale swresample sdl2", and ffplay.c includes SDL_thread.h. ffprobe brings its own textformat/ output modules (tf_json, tf_xml, tf_compact and friends) for machine-readable output.
  • Quirk of the tree itself: the default branch is master, HEAD was a948f8e34a21 at the time of writing, and the repository holds roughly 11,200 tracked files, with the six media libraries and fftools/ living as siblings at the top level.

Honest Limits

  • Every line number here was verified against master at commit a948f8e34a21 (checked 2026-11-13). FFmpeg moves fast, so expect drift — two moves are already visible on this branch: avcodec_receive_frame() now lives in libavcodec/avcodec.c, and avfilter_graph_config() is in libavfilter/avfiltergraph.c, not avfilter.c.
  • This tour covers the generic software path. Hardware acceleration (fftools/ffmpeg_hw.c), the per-container callbacks behind demux.c and mux.c, and the sub-second audio/video sync logic inside the SyncQueue are described only at the level this article needs.
  • No performance numbers are claimed anywhere on purpose: real fps depends on codec, filters, resolution and CPU. The sources show mechanics, not benchmarks.
  • -c copy bypasses most of the story via of_streamcopy() — demux straight to mux, no decode, no filter, no encode.
  • ffplay’s playback loop (window, audio clock sync) is a separate program sharing these libraries and is not covered here; it builds on SDL2 (configure line 4369), which we toured separately.

If you want to trace further on your own, ffprobe.c is the best API tutorial in the repository — a clean, standalone consumer of the same libraries. And the next time a 4K transcode hogs your CPU for an hour, you will know exactly which threads are to blame and where each one blocks.
entry.summary: What ffmpeg actually does frame by frame under a 4K transcode load: a line-linked tour through ffmpeg.c, the scheduler, libavformat, libavcodec and libavfilter on current master.

entry.title: Inside mpv’s playloop: the player core that skips frames instead of stuttering

link.title: Inside mpv’s playloop: the player core that skips frames instead of stuttering

entry.content:
Your video stalls for a tenth of a second, and most players respond by freezing the picture while the audio buffer runs dry — you get the ugly double-jerk of a paused frame followed by a sound hiccup. mpv almost never does this. When the machine cannot keep up, it quietly throws away frames that nobody would have seen anyway and keeps both the picture and the sound moving. That behavior is not an accident or a heuristic buried in a driver; it is the deliberate design of a very small amount of code in player/.

The second thing that surprises people is how old-school the architecture looks. There is one big C struct holding the whole player’s state, and one loop that ticks through it. There is no event framework, no actor system, no dependency injection — yet the demuxer, the decoders, the video output and the audio output all run as independent state machines that never block each other. If you enjoyed the decoder-centric tours of FFmpeg or the VLC playback core, this is the smaller, meaner cousin: same domain, radically fewer moving parts.

The third hook is the spacebar. You press it, the video freezes instantly — and when you press it again, sound resumes without a glitch even though the audio device has been sitting idle. The path between that keypress and the speaker runs through a dispatch queue, two handler functions, and a status variable called audio_status, and mpv’s authors have left comments along that path explaining exactly why each step exists. Let’s follow it.

Overview of mpv's playback architecture: one core thread runs run_playloop() forever, while the demuxer thread, the video-output thread and the audio device advance independently and wake the core when there is work to do.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts at mpv_main, L455, which builds the central struct MPContext, L244 — a single struct holding tracks, playback statuses, timing fields and the dispatch queue the whole core sleeps on.
  • The outer lifetime loop is mp_play_files, L2280: an endless for(;;) that idles when there is nothing to play, loads the next playlist entry, then hands control to the per-file loop.
  • Per file, play_current_file, L1811 opens the demuxer and then simply spins run_playloop, L2111 until stop_play says otherwise — the actual implementation of run_playloop, L1326 lives in playloop.c and is about seventy lines of straight-line handler calls.
  • Each tick calls fill_audio_out_buffers, L1344 before write_video, L1345: audio is deliberately serviced first, because the audio device is the clock everything else follows.
  • The video side pulls packets via demux_read_packet_async, L2973, which never blocks: if the background reader has not caught up yet, the decoder just waits and the core stays responsive.
  • That background reader is demux_thread, L2746, a dedicated thread that keeps packet queues filled ahead of playback so the presentation loop never waits on disk or network.
  • Finished frames are handed to vo_thread, L1117, which schedules presentation against vertical sync and counts every frame it had to drop.
  • Finally the tick ends with mp_wait_events, L1385, where the core parks itself on a dispatch queue — it only spins again when a thread, a timeout, or your keyboard wakes it.

The detail view opens run_playloop() into its handlers and follows each thread: demuxer internals on one side, the video chain with its drop accounting, the audio chain with underrun recovery, and the command path from keypress to state change.

Pressing space: from keypress to silence

When you hit space, the core is almost certainly inside mp_wait_events, L53 — asleep on mp_dispatch_queue_process() with an effectively infinite deadline. The input thread does not touch player state directly; it queues a command, and the next run of mp_process_input, L110 drains that queue, calling run_command, L5954 for each. Pausing is handled by set_pause_state, L165, and this is where the design shows its seams deliberately: the function pushes the new state outward — ao_set_paused() to the audio device, vo_set_paused() to the video output — then calls mp_wakeup_core() so the loop re-runs and notices.

The subtle part is what is remembered. In the unpause branch, the code subtracts the wall-clock time spent paused from the frame timer ((void)get_relative_time(mpctx); // ignore time that passed during pause). The frame that was on screen when you paused is still exactly where it was; video and audio have not drifted, because nothing kept running. On resume, handle_playback_restart, L1157 flips the chain statuses back to STATUS_PLAYING and calls audio_start_ao, L1184 only after both chains report ready — that is the comment-level contract: “Actual playback starts when both audio and video are ready” (write_video, L1100). One keypress, one wakeup, one status flip; no timers racing, no leftover buffers to flush.

First playback has one more stop on the way. The audio chain starts in STATUS_SYNCING (audio.c, L238): fill_audio_out_buffers, L943 refuses to declare victory until the device-side queue is actually full, at which point the status flips to STATUS_READY with the log line “audio ready” (audio.c, L946). Only then does the restart handler start the device. That is why mpv is silent for a beat on startup: it is deliberately buffering enough audio to survive a scheduling hiccup before the first sample is played, the same defensive philosophy behind the underrun recovery described below.

Why mpv skips frames instead of stuttering

The frame-dropping decision is made in two places that cooperate. Inside the core, check_framedrop, L354 runs while both audio and video are playing. It computes how many frames the decoder is behind — (mpctx->last_av_difference - 0.010) / frame_time, clamped to 0..100 — and tells the decoder wrapper to produce that many fewer frames. The code comments call it “a crappy heuristic; avoid getting upset by incorrect fps”, which is refreshingly honest: it bails out on suspicious container frame rates below 20 or above 500 rather than trying to be clever.

Downstream, the video-output thread does its own accounting at presentation time. In render_frame, L921, a frame whose end time has already passed is marked dropped_frame before it is ever drawn (vo.c, L959), the count is bumped at vo.c, L994, and wakeup_core() tells the playback loop to fetch the next frame immediately. Dropping a frame costs one missed presentation slot; stuttering costs an audible underrun and a visible freeze. The core even measures the audio side for trouble: fill_audio_out_buffers, L969 logs “Audio device underrun detected” and restarts the device rather than pretending nothing happened. Fine-grained A/V correction is separate again — adjust_sync, L382 nudges the internal delay toward the audio timeline by a bounded amount per frame, so small clock drift is absorbed invisibly while large gaps trigger the drop path instead.

The demuxer: a thread that is always ahead

The demuxer is the reason the rest of the player can be simple. demux_start_thread, L1237 spawns demux_thread, L2746, whose loop is three lines: do one unit of thread_work, L2707 — read a packet via read_packet, L2323, execute a queued seek, switch tracks, or update caches — and if there was nothing to do, sleep until the next cache maintenance deadline. The reader-side state, struct demux_internal at demux.c, L165, owns the packet queues and the locking; the core only ever pulls from them through the non-blocking async API and inspects snapshots through demux_get_reader_state, L4873 (the same snapshot the EOF handler at handle_eof, L1279 consults before ending a file).

Memory does not grow without bound: prune_old_packets, L2464 discards packets behind the reader unless you explicitly asked for caching, and update_cache, L4527 maintains the seekable byte ranges that make a backward seek instant. This is the same division of labor you can see in FFmpeg’s own I/O layer and in VLC’s input manager — but mpv keeps it in one 5000-line file instead of a framework.

Worth noting is what all of this is not: it is not a busy poller. When thread_work, L2755 reports nothing to do, the demuxer thread sleeps on a condition variable until the next cache-maintenance deadline (demux.c, L2758). The core applies the same trick in reverse — several handlers set bounded timeouts like 0.1 or 0.2 seconds via mp_set_timeout, L74 (L691, L785) — but a timeout is always the fallback, never the signal path. Producers call wakeups: packets arriving, a frame finishing presentation, a vsync interrupt, all of them end in wakeup_core() rather than in waiting out a timer. That is how one core thread can serve audio, video, subtitles, OSD and input without ever burning a CPU core while a movie plays.

From player/core.c to player/main.c

Every source tour runs into drift, and this one ran into a notable piece: the legendary player/core.c no longer exists on master. The entry point and lifecycle functions (mpv_main, mp_create, mp_initialize) live in player/main.c, the central MPContext struct lives in player/core.h, and the file-loading logic moved into loadfile.c. Anyone following old blog posts or stack-overflow answers that cite core.c will be chasing a ghost — the line numbers in this post were all verified against the current tree.

Build facts observed during the tour, straight from the tree:

  • The project targets version 0.42.0-UNKNOWN per the root MPV_VERSION file — the -UNKNOWN suffix signals a non-release checkout, exactly what you get cloning master.
  • The build is meson-only: the root meson.build, L1 declares the project with meson_version: '>=1.3.0' at L6, and there is no configure script or alternative build system anywhere in the tree.
  • FFmpeg is the load-bearing dependency with pinned floors: libavcodec >= 60.31.102 (L23), libavformat >= 60.16.100 (L25), libavutil >= 58.29.100 (L26), libswresample >= 4.12.100 (L27), plus libass >= 0.12.2 for subtitle rendering at L33.
  • Subproject fallbacks are enabled for ffmpeg and libass (L49-L51), so a fresh clone can build its own copies instead of hunting system packages — a pattern worth copying if you maintain C projects that depend on fast-moving libraries.

If you want to see how other projects in this space structure the same problem, the FFmpeg tour covers the decoding libraries underneath mpv, the VLC tour covers a much larger player framework, and the Alacritty tour is a good contrast in terminal-side vsync handling.

Honest Limits

  • Everything here reflects commit fe753a782461 (master, November 2026). mpv moves fast; run_playloop’s handler list and the demuxer internals have been reshuffled repeatedly in the past, so re-verify line numbers before citing them in a patch or bug report.
  • The frame-drop heuristic in check_framedrop only applies to ordinary playback with audio as the clock: the source gates it on opts->frame_dropping & 2, both chains playing, and sane container fps, so --audio-only files, untimed audio outputs, and display-sync modes follow different timing paths not covered in this post.
  • The exact behavior of pause/resume depends on your audio driver: ao_set_paused() is defined in audio/out/buffer.c, and pull-style or untimed AOs handle the paused state differently from push-style ones; the underrun-recovery code even carries a comment “(Buggy if AO underruns.)” for the gapless case.
  • This tour is deliberately single-file deep. The Lua/JavaScript client API, the --vo=gpu-next render abstraction, and hardware decoding each have their own subdirectories and were not covered here.
entry.summary: A source tour of the mpv player core: run_playloop, the demuxer thread, the video chain, frame dropping, and what happens between pressing space and hearing audio.

entry.title: OBS Studio source tour: where a dropped frame actually dies in libobs

link.title: OBS Studio source tour: where a dropped frame actually dies in libobs

entry.content:
Your stream sits at 20 fps. The OBS stats window says “skipped frames due to rendering lag,” your GPU is nowhere near 100%, and none of your sources report errors. You are not alone in finding this maddening, because the answer is not in the settings dialog at all — it is one specific line inside libobs, the C core underneath the OBS Studio frontend, where a frame that missed its deadline gets quietly converted into a counter increment and forgotten. Once you have seen that line, “rendering lag” stops being a mystery and becomes a measurement problem.

libobs is not a media player and not a compositor in the browser sense. It is a small, strict real-time scheduler: exactly one graphics thread wakes up at your configured frame interval — 33.3 ms at 30 fps, 16.6 ms at 60 — walks a composable graph of sources and scenes, renders the whole stack into one texture, stages it for encoders, and then tries to sleep precisely until the next deadline. Audio runs on a completely separate thread that never touches the GPU, mixing 1024-frame chunks of PCM on its own wall-clock rhythm. The two paths only meet at the output, right before encoding.

This tour walks the master branch of obsproject/obs-studio the way a frame would travel: from int main in the Qt frontend, through the single graphics thread loop, down the scene render chain to individual draw calls, and out toward encoders and outputs. Every symbol below was verified against the actual tree — including one rename that trips up older documentation. If you enjoy this kind of tour, we have done the same for FFmpeg, SDL, and Godot on this site; links are sprinkled where they help.

The libobs core at a glance: one Qt frontend, one 60 Hz graphics thread, one independent audio mixer thread, and outputs that consume both streams.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The process starts in ordinary Qt territory: main, L887 parses command-line arguments, installs crash handling, and constructs the OBSApp Qt object before any OBS-specific machinery exists.
  • The frontend then boots the core with obs_startup, L1330, which is deliberately one-shot — call it twice and it logs a warning and refuses.
  • Video bring-up happens in obs_init_video, L695, which builds the canvas and video mixes, and then spawns the graphics thread, L720 with a plain pthread_create.
  • That thread’s body is obs_graphics_thread, L1161, a while loop over obs_graphics_thread_loop, L1097 — the heartbeat of the whole program.
  • Each iteration first ticks every source via tick_sources, L32, which calls obs_source_video_tick, L82 on each source in the main list.
  • Rendering is orchestrated by output_frame, L871, which calls render_video, L541 and then downloads or hands off the finished texture.
  • The actual pixel work bottoms out in scene_video_render, L1059, which walks the scene’s linked list of items and draws each visible one.
  • After rendering, video_sleep, L808 targets the next frame deadline; a missed target is where lagged frames are born.
  • Audio never joins this loop: audio_thread, L205 sleeps to its own deadlines and emits mixed PCM in fixed chunks.

The detail view: the init sequence on the left, the graphics-thread loop in the middle (tick chain, render chain, sleep and FPS accounting), the audio thread at the bottom, and the output capture path on the right.

The heartbeat: one graphics thread, one loop

The most important architectural decision in libobs is that there is exactly one thread that renders. obs_graphics_thread, L1161 sets a thread name (“libobs: graphics thread”), computes the frame interval once, and then loops. Inside obs_graphics_thread_loop, L1097 the per-frame order is fixed: update active states, tick sources at tick_sources, L1112, pump the render pass through output_frames, L1125, paint preview windows with render_displays, L94, execute queued graphics tasks, and only then sleep.

One consequence: everything shares one frame budget. A heavy source filter, a slow capture device, and even an expensive preview paint all draw from the same 16.6 ms allowance. This is a different shape from SDL, where you own the loop yourself, and from Godot, where the engine separates process and render phases — see our Godot scene-tree tour. libobs gives you neither: the loop is fixed, and your sources are guests inside it.

Where a 20 fps stream actually dies

Here is the line you came for. video_sleep, L808 computes the next deadline as cur_time + interval_ns and calls os_sleepto_ns, L815. If the sleep succeeds, one frame was produced on schedule. If it fails — meaning the tick-plus-render work already overran the interval — the function counts how many whole intervals were missed, and records them: lagged_frames, L828 adds count - 1 to the mix’s running total. That counter is what surfaces later as “lagged frames” in the frontend’s statistics.

Note what this implies for your 20 fps mystery. Frames are not “dropped” by the encoder at that point; they die before encoding, in the pacing function, because the loop arrived late. The per-second bookkeeping that publishes the measured rate happens just after the sleep, in the FPS accounting block at video_fps, L1149. So the diagnostic order is: if lagged frames rise while the GPU is idle, something in the tick or render path is blocking on the CPU (a slow source callback, a lock, disk I/O in a filter); if lagged frames rise with the GPU saturated, you are simply asking for more pixels than the machine can rasterize in one interval.

Scenes are just sources: the render chain

The composable part of libobs is elegant. A scene is itself an obs_source — obs_scene_create, L1794 returns an ordinary source handle — which means scenes nest inside scenes and the renderer does not care. When the graphics thread needs pixels, render_main_texture, L172 clears the render target, runs any registered draw callbacks, and then calls obs_view_render, L202. The view walks its fixed set of channels — obs_view_render, L118 iterates MAX_CHANNELS slots — and calls obs_source_video_render, L135 on whatever source is bound to each.

For a scene source, that dispatch lands in scene_video_render, L1059, which takes the video lock, then walks the first_item linked list at scene items loop, L1077 and calls render_item on each visible entry. Every draw goes through the effect system: an effect is a shader bundle whose parameters are looked up with gs_effect_get_param_by_name, L275 and uploaded with setters like gs_effect_set_float, L436. After the main texture exists, render_convert_texture, L566 converts RGBA to planar YUV on the GPU — a step our FFmpeg tour revisits from the other side, where encoders consume exactly that planar layout.

The tick side mirrors the render side. obs_source_video_tick, L1406 handles async video buffers, audio action queues, and filter timing for every source, and a scene’s own scene_video_tick, L990 advances item transforms and visibility transitions. Tick and render are deliberately decoupled: state mutates during the tick, then is read to paint during the render pass.

Audio never touches the graphics thread

Audio is the second half of the story and runs on its own clock. During startup, obs_init_audio, L907 configures sample rate and speaker layout and opens the audio subsystem through audio_output_open, L353, which spawns its thread at pthread_create, L376. That thread is audio_thread, L205: an infinite loop that computes a wall-clock deadline 1024 samples ahead — the chunk size is the compile-time constant AUDIO_OUTPUT_FRAMES, L31 — sleeps to it with a fast path at os_sleepto_ns_fast, L227, and then runs input_and_output, L160.

The mixing itself is refreshingly boring: sum every registered input’s float planes into a mix buffer, clamp, convert to the output format, and invoke the registered callback — once per mix, per chunk. Because deadlines are wall-clock anchored rather than “1024 samples after the last work finished,” a slow mixing pass does not accumulate drift; it either makes the deadline or the buffer underruns audibly. On Windows the thread even registers itself with MMCSS via AvSetMmThreadCharacteristics so the scheduler treats it gently. This is the same separation of clocks we saw in the FFmpeg scheduling model: video paced by frame intervals, audio paced by sample counts, reconciled only at the mux — start there.

From CMake presets to pixels

Building OBS from source tells you a lot about how the core is organized. The root CMakeLists.txt, L1 demands CMake 3.28–3.30 — a notably modern floor — and pulls in a bootstrap script from cmake/common/ before the project is even declared. The component layout is explicit: ENABLE_FRONTEND, L18 gates the Qt UI (it requires Qt and can be switched off to build headless libobs consumers), and the renderer backends are separate plugins: libobs-d3d11, L24 plus libobs-winrt on Windows, libobs-opengl, L27 elsewhere, libobs-metal, L29 on macOS. The frontend is added last, at add_subdirectory(frontend), L35.

One fact worth flagging for anyone following old tutorials: the Qt code no longer lives in a top-level UI/ directory. It moved to frontend/, the class is OBSApp (constructor at OBSApp::OBSApp, L959), and the entry point moved with it into frontend/obs-main.cpp. For this tour we cloned the repository sparsely (only libobs, frontend, and cmake), which yielded roughly 5,700 tracked paths total and made grepping the C core comfortable on a laptop.

Honest Limits

  • Line numbers refer to the master branch as cloned on 2026-11-13 (commit fe1ed7955f30). The GitHub blob/master/ links above will drift as files are edited; symbols are stable, lines are not.
  • Older documentation and some third-party diagrams mention a function named obs_video_tick. It no longer exists in master; the loop is obs_graphics_thread_loop. We re-derived the tick path from the tree rather than trusting prior art.
  • The diagrams trace the core frame path only. Encoder internals (x264, NVENC, the encoder-group logic visible around video_sleep), plugin sources like display/window capture, and the scripting layer live outside the traced files and are not covered.
  • The audio section describes the audio-io thread’s pacing and mixing; the deeper per-source audio path (timestamp offsets and buffering on the way into the mixer) is a separate libobs file we did not verify line-by-line for this tour.
  • “Rendering lag” has other contributors we deliberately excluded: GPU driver behavior, VSync interactions of the preview, and Windows-specific timer resolution are real but not observable from this repository alone.
entry.summary: A guided walk through OBS Studio's libobs core in C: the 60 Hz graphics thread, the scene render chain, the separate audio mixer thread, and the exact line where lagged frames are counted.

entry.title: VLC Source Tour: One Binary That Plays Everything, Built From Loadable Parts

link.title: VLC Source Tour: One Binary That Plays Everything, Built From Loadable Parts

entry.content:
You hand VLC a strange file — a 4 GB ISO, an HLS playlist from a network camera, a half-corrupted AVI — and it just plays. No codec pack, no “install a plugin to continue”, no format picker. The usual guess is that VLC secretly bundles a monster table of every format ever invented. The source tree says otherwise: almost nothing is built in.

On master (4.0.0-dev), the modules/ directory alone holds 848 .c files across 30 subdirectories: 94 demuxers, 114 codecs, 51 access drivers. Each one declares a capability string and a score, and the core discovers them at startup by scanning a plugins directory. The core does not know what an MP4 is; it knows how to ask “who can demux this?” and probe candidates in score order until one claims the stream.

This tour walks that machinery end to end — entry point, module bank, input thread, decoder threads, audio and video outputs — using line-numbered links into the master tree. Two diagrams map the same structure: the first shows the whole shape, the second zooms into the layers where modules actually get swapped in.

Overview of the VLC media engine on master. Every arrow that crosses from the core into a subsystem passes through one of two functions: module_need() or vlc_module_load(). That choke point is the whole trick.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main() in bin/vlc.c, L117 blocks signals, calls libvlc_new, L239, starts an interface via libvlc_InternalAddIntf, L248, then libvlc_InternalPlay, L254 and parks itself in sigwait, L268.
  • libvlc_InternalInit, L130 in src/libvlc.c boots the module bank at module_InitBank, L146 and loads plugins at module_LoadPlugins, L162 — all before command line parsing at config_LoadCmdLine, L169, because plugins contribute their own options.
  • module_LoadPlugins, L803 registers static builtins via module_InitStatic, L166 and scans the plugin directory through AllocateAllPlugins, L570, where AllocatePluginFile, L313 hands each candidate to module_InitDynamic, L260.
  • Every lookup funnels into vlc_module_load, L195, ranked by vlc_module_match, L110, which sorts candidates by decreasing score at L174-177. module_need, L268 is the object-level wrapper.
  • vlc_player_Start, L1228 may open the next media directly at L1264 via vlc_player_OpenNextMedia, L56, spawning an input thread through input_Start, L124.
  • The input thread body Run, L407 runs Init, L1293, builds the access stream with stream_AccessNew, L283 whose module_need(‘access’), L141 picks file/http/dshow, then hands the stream to demux_NewAdvanced, L2803.
  • demux_NewAdvanced, L118 sniffs MIME at L171 and file extension at L182 before probing candidates with vlc_module_load(‘demux’), L196.
  • Elementary stream records land in input_EsOutNew, L4414; EsOutCreateDecoder, L2578 spawns a per-ES decoder via CreateDecoder, L2163 running DecoderThread, L1976.
  • Codecs load through decoder_LoadModule, L56 using module_need_var, L86; outputs come from aout_New, L264 and vout_Create, L2205.

Detailed view: the module bank on the left feeds every consumer on the right. The MP4 demuxer and the avcodec codec are shown as concrete examples of modules being probed, loaded, and — when formats change mid-playback — reloaded.

Every subsystem is a capability lookup

The unit of modularity is the module descriptor, not the shared object. A plugin file is opened by module_InitDynamic, L260, and its entry registers one or more descriptors declared with the vlc_module_begin() macro, L333. Each descriptor carries a capability via set_capability, L381 and entry callbacks via set_callbacks, L390. Builtins skip the dynamic load entirely: module_InitStatic, L166 registers whatever the build compiled in, and the core itself is one of them (VLC_MODULE_ENTRY(core), L735).

Lookup has exactly one shape everywhere. vlc_module_match, L110 collects candidates for a capability: the shortcuts “none” (L142) and “any” (L148) are handled first, then everything else is appended in decreasing score order. vlc_module_load, L195 walks that ranked list and probes each candidate (L230), telling each one whether it was an explicit user pick or a scored guess. module_need, L268 wraps this for objects.

The loop itself tolerates failure gracefully. Candidates are mapped and probed one by one (L219-230), and only VLC_SUCCESS — or a timeout at L239 — stops the walk; anything else simply falls through to the next name in the ranked list. That quiet fall-through is the heart of “plays everything”: format detection is not one clever guess but many cheap failures.

Even the GUI obeys. libvlc_InternalAddIntf, L202 ends in module_need(p_intf, ‘interface’), L112 — the Qt interface is just the highest-scoring “interface” module the bank happens to contain.

The cleanest single-file example is the avcodec plugin: vlc_module_begin, L80 registers four decoder submodules — “video decoder” score 70 (L89), a hardware shortcut “ffmpeghw” at 10001 (L94), “audio decoder” (L99) and “spu decoder” (L104). One plugin file, four capabilities, and the actual decode work happens in OpenVideoCodec, L487 inside libavcodec — which is exactly what makes the binary small and the codec coverage huge. Our FFmpeg source tour picks up that story on the library side of the boundary: /ffmpeg/.

The input thread: from URL to elementary streams

vlc_player_Start, L1228 guards its started state and hands the media to the input core. input_Start, L124 spawns a thread whose body, Run, L407, first runs Init, L1293 and only then enters MainLoop, L649.

Init builds the source chain. An access module yields bytes: stream_AccessNew, L283 wraps access_New, L88, and module_need(access, ‘access’), L141 is where “file”, “http”, or a webcam driver wins. Filters can then be stacked on the stream — a record filter for capture is appended at L2800 — before the demuxer sees anything.

Demuxer selection starts with sniffing, not scores. demux_NewAdvanced, L118 asks the stream’s MIME type (L171) and, if the URL carries a file extension, builds an “ext-XXX” hint (L182). Only then does vlc_module_load(‘demux’), L196 probe candidates. The MP4 demuxer registers at score 240 (L74) with a fallback variant at 239 (L90); the higher score is probed first, and its Open, L1001 claims the stream by successfully parsing boxes. Once playing, MainLoop, L649 drains user commands through ControlPop, L754 — seeks, pause, rate changes — while each demux cycle pushes elementary stream records into the es_out.

A decoder thread per elementary stream

The es_out is the seam between the format world and the codec world. input_EsOutNew, L4414 creates the sink every demuxer receives. When a track appears, EsOutCreateDecoder, L2578 calls CreateDecoder, L2163, which builds a fifo, optionally a packetizer via LoadDecoder, L2284, and spawns DecoderThread, L1976 — named “vlc-dec-video”, “vlc-dec-audio” or “vlc-dec-spu” depending on category (L1983).

The codec module itself loads inside that thread: LoadDecoder, L524 calls decoder_LoadModule, L56, which runs module_need_var, L86 — and the capability is literally the ES category. Decoder choice is the same score-ordered probe as demuxer choice; there is no separate codec dispatch layer.

The same per-thread loop owns flushing and pause. While the thread lives it checks a flushing flag first and runs DecoderThread_Flush, L2003 before touching anything else, which is what keeps picture and sound coherent when you scrub through a stream.

Threads can rebuild themselves mid-playback. DecoderThread_Reload, L538 tears the codec down and re-runs LoadDecoder, L576 when, for instance, the audio output requests a restart. Frames flow through DecoderThread_DecodeBlock, L1783, including an optional packetizer pass at L1878, then fan out to the outputs: audio to aout_New, L264 where module_need_var(‘audio output’), L303 picks a platform sink, video to vout_Create, L2205 whose display is matched by vlc_module_match(‘vout display’), L878 inside vout_display_New, L828, with format converters assembled through a filter chain (L323). If you want to compare another window-and-audio layer, our SDL tour covers SDL’s output abstractions: /sdl/.

From autotools to meson (and a side of Rust)

A few build facts straight from the master tree, observed while reading:

  • Version: configure.ac, L5 declares AC_INIT([vlc], [4.0.0-dev]), with a copyright banner reading 1999-2026 at L3.
  • Two build systems ship together. The classic ./bootstrap script runs autoreconf (with bundled tools from extras/tools/build) while a full meson.build, L2 coexists in-tree, pinning c_std=gnu17 and cpp_std=c++17 at L3, a codename of Otto Chriek at L7, and libvlc_abi_version = '12.0.0' at L11.
  • Rust is entering at the edges. A Cargo workspace (Cargo.toml, L3) holds vlcrs-core, vlcrs-macros, vlcrs-messages and vlcrs-utils under src/rust/, plus a Telegraf logger module at L7 — pinned to channel = "nightly" in rust-toolchain.toml, L2. Building the Rust bits from source genuinely needs a nightly toolchain, not just a stable one.
  • Scale check from my clone: 848 .c files under modules/ (94 demux, 114 codec, 51 access), and 6368 tree entries at depth 1 with a blob-less partial clone. For reading, I checked out only bin/, src/, modules/, include/ and lib/; the build files quoted here are single root-level files pulled on demand with git show.
  • The Rust edge modules are a deliberate contrast to a fully Rust-native codebase like Alacritty, which owns its whole stack: /alacritty/.

Honest Limits

Only caveats that the repository itself supports:

  • Probing is heuristic, not declarative. Nothing in the core “knows” MP4; the format is claimed by whichever candidate’s Open() succeeds first in score order. A greedy demuxer can shadow better ones, and the fallback variant at score 239 (mp4.c, L90) exists precisely because one descriptor per format is not always enough.
  • Naming a module by shortcut overrides the scores. An explicit match is probed first and forced (generic_start, L254; probe flag at L230), which is how “ffmpeghw” at score 10001 (avcodec.c, L94) beats the software path whenever requested.
  • Plugin discovery is path-based, not registry-based. AllocateAllPlugins, L570 walks directories, and a dev build points VLC_PLUGIN_PATH at the build tree (bin/vlc.c, L143). A broken install layout means mysteriously missing codecs.
  • Not everything is a module. The input thread, es_out and player are compiled into the core; the module boundary sits only at access, demux, codec, audio output, video output and interface.
  • The cost model is one fifo thread per elementary stream (L1976). A many-track file spawns accordingly — fine on desktop, worth knowing on constrained hardware.
  • master is a moving target: 4.0.0-dev with ABI 12.0.0 (meson.build, L11) and two build systems mid-migration. The line numbers above were true on the day of this post and may drift.
entry.summary: How videolan/vlc opens a network stream, an ISO, and a webcam with no codec pack: the module bank, capability scores, demuxer probing, and per-stream decoder threads, verified line by line on master.

entry.title: Inside Bevy: How the ECS Scheduler Runs Your Systems in Parallel

link.title: Inside Bevy: How the ECS Scheduler Runs Your Systems in Parallel

entry.content:
Every engine built around a god-object eventually hits the same wall. A GameObject grows a transform, a mesh, a collider, a health value, a script slot, and suddenly every subsystem walks a pointer-chasing object graph, and “can this object move during this phase?” becomes a tribal-knowledge question. Bevy — the data-oriented game engine written in Rust — refuses that design. State lives in flat tables, behavior lives in plain functions, and the compiler enforces who may read or write what. If you have read our tour of Godot, this is the opposite philosophy: no scene tree as the center of the world, just entities and component sets.

So what actually happens on one frame tick? A runner wakes up, a handful of labeled schedules execute in order, each schedule fans its systems out across worker threads, then the render side extracts what it needs and submits GPU commands. Every step is ordinary Rust code you can read in the repository, and the interesting parts are all struct-level decisions: how storage is laid out, how queries cache their results, and where the scheduler inserts synchronization points.

The third question is the boldest: how can thousands of systems mutate the same world concurrently without locks? Bevy’s answer is that it never needs a global lock, because each system declares its data access up front. The scheduler computes disjoint borrows from those declarations and only runs systems in parallel when their accesses provably do not conflict — much friendlier to multicore than, say, a GC runtime where everything shares one heap, like the GIL situation we covered for CPython.

Bevy at a glance: the App drives labeled schedules over a World; archetypal storage feeds cached queries; the executor runs systems in parallel; a render sub-app and the asset server run beside the main loop.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The whole engine is one builder object. App, L85 owns the main World and the plugin registry; when you call App::run, L185 the App hands itself to a runner function, which for windowed apps is the winit event loop and never returns.
  • A frame is not one function call but a sequence of labeled schedules. Update, L173 sits between PreUpdate and PostUpdate, with Startup and First/Last bookending the loop — all defined in one readable file.
  • The World struct, L96 is the only place state lives. Spawning takes a Bundle, L1243 — a tuple of components — and returns a handle.
  • Storage is archetypal: Archetypes, L777 keeps exactly one archetype per unique component combination, so entities with the same shape sit in contiguous memory.
  • Each archetype points into columnar Tables, L203; components that churn get parked in SparseSets, L780 instead.
  • Queries do not scan the World each frame. QueryState, L85 caches the matched archetype list once and reuses it, which is why iteration cost stays proportional to live matches.
  • The Schedule struct, L413 turns your .before()/.after() hints into an ordering graph, then Schedule::run, L596 executes it — on native platforms via the MultiThreadedExecutor, L86.
  • Rendering is a sub-app, not a phase inside the main loop: RenderApp, L381 gets its own World, and the RenderGraph schedule, L48 chains Begin → Render → Submit → Finish inside it.
  • Assets stream in without blocking: AssetServer::load, L364 returns a typed handle immediately and fills the Assets<T> resource when bytes arrive.

The detail view: how spawning moves entities between archetypes, how the executor splits world borrows, and how the render sub-app and asset server plug into the same World primitives.

One Frame in Bevy: Runner, Sub-Apps, and Schedules

Bevy’s entry point looks deceptively small: App::new().add_plugins(DefaultPlugins).run(). The magic is that a plugin is just data plus a build function — the Plugin trait, L57 requires exactly one build(&mut App) method — so “adding a plugin” means “run its registrations against the App now”, not registering a factory for later.

App::run does something unusual: it mem::replaces the App with an empty one and passes the real App to the stored runner closure. The default runner is the ScheduleRunnerPlugin, L50, a headless loop; winit swaps it for a platform event loop. Either way, each tick calls App::update, L158, which simply calls update() on every SubApp, L66 — the main app first, then the render app.

Why sub-apps? Because the main world and the render world must never fight over the same borrow. App::add_systems, L321 targets the main app’s schedules, while render systems live in the RenderApp’s separate schedule set, each side holding a World that is structurally independent.

Archetypes and Queries: Storage as Columns

Spawning a Bundle does not allocate a heap object. The World finds (or creates) the archetype for that exact component combination, appends each component to its table column, and records the entity’s row location. Adding or removing a component moves the entity to a different archetype — a copy of a few dozen bytes plus an index fix-up, not a rebuild. Hot component data therefore streams through memory like a database scan, which is precisely what makes the ECS fast; this is the data-oriented design that only a language with explicit ownership, like Rust, can hand you without a garbage collector pausing mid-frame.

Archetypes and tables are deliberately decoupled: multiple archetypes can share one table when they differ only in sparse-set components. One quirk worth knowing: archetypes are never cleaned up. The module docs in archetype.rs, L14 note that empty archetypes persist until the World is dropped — so code that rapidly creates unique component combinations accumulates empty shells rather than freeing them. The World even exposes a convenience method that builds and caches a query in one call at World::query, L1862.

The query side is where most engines waste cycles. Bevy’s Query, L488 parameter is paired with a cached state object, initialized once via QueryState::new, L249. That state remembers which archetypes and tables match, so per-frame iteration (QueryState::iter, L1223) walks precomputed lists instead of re-filtering every entity. When a new archetype appears mid-run, the state picks it up and revalidates — an incremental update, not a full rebuild.

The Parallel Scheduler, Sync Points, and Change Ticks

When a schedule builds, each system’s declared Query parameters produce an access fingerprint. Systems whose accesses overlap get ordered relative to each other; systems with disjoint accesses become candidates for parallel execution. At run time the default_executor, L48 picks the multi-threaded path on native platforms, and the executor spawns one task per ready system — you can see the task-per-system pattern at spawn_system_task, L638. No mutex guards the World; instead, systems receive an UnsafeWorldCell whose disjoint-borrow contract the scheduler has already proven.

Two subtleties keep this honest. First, structural changes (spawn, despawn, component add) are deferred: a system queues Commands and applies them later, and Bevy auto-inserts sync points for this — the auto_insert_apply_deferred setting, L1913 controls it, and apply_deferred, L722 is the flush. A sync point is a barrier: systems after it can observe the new state, systems before it ran in parallel underneath.

Second, change detection is just counters. Every component carries Tick, L23 stamps for when it was added and last changed, and the DetectChanges trait, L11 exposes is_changed(). Filters like Changed<T>, L1092 compare those stamps, so “run only when input changed” costs one integer comparison per entity.

The Render Sub-App and Streaming Assets

Rendering runs on its own clock. The RenderPlugin, L161 creates the render sub-app, initializes GPU resources in a RenderStartup schedule, and every frame the extraction step — now factored into its own crate, bevy_extract, L16 — copies just what this frame needs from the main world into the render world. The GPU work itself rides on wgpu, L27, so Vulkan, Metal, and DirectX share one code path; the same backend powers GPU-terminal projects like Alacritty.

Assets follow the same “don’t block” logic. AssetServer::load hands back a Handle, L115 immediately; loaders run through a pluggable IO layer (filesystem, embedded, memory, web), and the Assets<A>, L288 resource resolves handles to loaded data. Any type implementing the Asset trait, L456 gets the whole machinery for free. Because entities hold handles rather than asset data, a texture can still be loading while gameplay code runs — systems simply observe an empty slot until the load completes.

From Cargo Build to First Frame

The repo is a Cargo workspace whose members are declared as crates/* — the ECS, the renderer, and every subsystem are independent crates you can read in isolation. To try it: clone the repo, git checkout latest (a moving tag pointing at the newest release), then cargo run --example breakout — the full arcade game lives at examples/showcase/breakout.rs. For something minimal, examples/3d/3d_scene.rs draws a lit 3D scene in roughly sixty lines. The README’s “hello window” is exactly four statements: App::new().add_plugins(DefaultPlugins).run().

Two build knobs matter in practice. The dynamic_linking feature (declared in crates/bevy_internal/Cargo.toml) turns each crate into a dylib so incremental rebuilds skip relinking the engine; and the multi_threaded feature is what selects the parallel executor — on Wasm the build falls back to the single-threaded one, per default_executor. The full feature matrix is documented in docs/cargo_features.md in the repo root. A plain cargo run --example breakout on a modern desktop takes a few minutes the first time (wgpu and its backends are heavy), then seconds per example afterward.

Honest Limits

Bevy’s README states plainly that it is in the early stages of development, with important features missing, sparse documentation, and breaking changes roughly every three months via the “train” release schedule. The main branch we toured is development code: a large part of the renderer was being reorganized around the render-graph-as-schedule design described in renderer/mod.rs, and extraction was recently pulled into the separate bevy_extract crate — expect churn if you follow along on main.

The engine is also honest about platform gaps: without the multi_threaded feature, or on Wasm, the executor degrades to single-threaded, and App::run never returns on iOS and Web because the platform event loop owns the thread. There is no stable plugin marketplace story and no built-in editor; you compose crates by hand. Development questions route to GitHub Discussions and the Contributor’s Guide in the repo root rather than a formal RFC board, which tells you how young the project still is. None of that blocks studying the code — it just means the architecture you read today may look different next release, and the migration guides at bevy.org are the companion reading this tour assumes.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Bevy's ECS: archetypal storage, cached queries, the parallel schedule executor, the render sub-app, and streaming assets.

entry.title: Inside Godot: How the Scene Tree, Servers, and GDScript VM Actually Work

link.title: Inside Godot: How the Scene Tree, Servers, and GDScript VM Actually Work

entry.content:
You write a small func _process(delta) in GDScript, press play, and a character moves across the screen at a smooth sixty frames per second. It feels like magic, but the whole thing is a precisely choreographed C++ routine that runs inside main/main.cpp on every tick: it splits elapsed wall-clock time into fixed physics steps and one fractional render step, walks your scene tree, drains a queue of rendering commands, swaps GPU buffers, and only then sleeps until the next frame. This post walks that exact path through the engine’s master branch (version 4.8.0, status beta, per version.py), because the best way to stop treating an engine as a black box is to read the loop that never stops running.

The first thing that confuses newcomers is the word “server” everywhere in the tree: RenderingServer, PhysicsServer3D, AudioServer, XRServer, even an AccessibilityServer under servers/display/. For an engine with no networking in sight, that naming looks wrong — until you see what it buys. Nodes never hold GPU handles or solver state. They push opaque resource IDs (RIDs) plus commands into a queue owned by the server, and the server decides when, and on which thread, that work actually executes. It is a client-server split drawn inside one process, which is why the engine can move rendering off the main thread with a boolean instead of a rewrite.

The second surprise is GDScript itself. There is no compile button and no separate build step for your scripts, yet scripts do not run as interpreted text trees either. When a .gd file loads, it is tokenized, parsed into an AST, type-checked, and lowered to a compact bytecode that a register-less Variant-stack VM executes — an interpreter loop in the same spirit as the C eval loop behind /cpython/, except it lives inside the game process and talks directly to engine singletons. Understanding those three mechanisms — the frame loop, the server layer, and the VM — explains almost every “why is it built this way” question you will have about Godot.

Overview of a Godot frame: boot hands control to Main::iteration, which drives the scene tree and the server layer; GDScript bytecode runs inside node callbacks, and physics backends plug in behind an abstract server.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Boot happens in two phases: Main::setup, L986 parses arguments and registers types, then Main::start, L4056 creates the main loop and loads your project’s main scene.
  • Every frame is one call to Main::iteration, L4967 — physics ticks first, one process pass, then sync and draw.
  • MainTimerSync, L4984 decides how many fixed physics steps this frame owes and what fraction of a step the render pass gets.
  • The scene side is a single SceneTree object whose physics_process, L640 and process, L689 methods fan work out to nodes through process groups.
  • PhysicsServer3D, L391 is a pure abstract interface — step, sync, flush_queries — with the default implementation living in a module.
  • The default solver, GodotPhysicsServer3D::step, L1693, is registered as a plugin; a Jolt backend sits beside it.
  • On the render side, RenderingServerDefault::_draw, L76 is the only place where the frame actually becomes pixels.
  • Script behavior enters the loop at GDScriptFunction::call, L465, the bytecode interpreter that every _process override ultimately runs on.

The same frame in detail: how SceneTree groups and dispatches notifications, how the rendering command queue is drained and executed, and how a GDScript file becomes bytecode before it ever runs.

The Frame: What Happens in One Main::iteration

Main::iteration is the heartbeat, and its ordering is deliberate. After MainTimerSync::advance, L4984 converts elapsed microseconds into an integer count of physics steps plus a fractional process_step, a loop at L5016 runs once per physics tick: it flushes buffered input, syncs the physics servers and flushes their queries (L5036), calls into the main loop’s physics_process (L5047), and finally steps both 2D and 3D solvers (L5081). Physics runs zero, one, or several times per frame — whatever keeps simulation time aligned with real time — while _process runs exactly once.

Then comes the visible half. A single main_loop->process() call at L5108 walks the idle pass, after which RenderingServer::sync() at L5123 drains queued commands and draw() at L5139 produces the frame. Housekeeping follows: GDExtensions tick at L5154, each registered script language gets its per-frame hook at L5158, and AudioServer::update, L1359 mixes the audio graph at L5162. Only at the very end does OS::add_frame_delay, L5228 sleep or spin to hit the target frame rate. If you have ever wondered why a slow _physics_process cascades worse than a slow _process, this order is the answer: physics debt accumulates in fixed chunks, capped by max_physics_steps_per_frame right before the loop.

The Scene Tree Dispatches Notifications, Not Magic

SceneTree is just the MainLoop implementation the engine installs by default, and it does not call your methods directly. It owns ProcessGroup structures; SceneTree::_process, L1260 reorders dirty groups, and SceneTree::_process_group, L1193 does the real work: it sorts nodes by their configured priority, takes a defensive copy of the node list (L1217) so nodes can add or remove themselves mid-iteration, then walks the copy sending notifications — NOTIFICATION_PHYSICS_PROCESS at L1239 or NOTIFICATION_PROCESS at L1246. Nodes that pause or leave the tree are skipped via a can_process() check, which is how the pause menu freezes your game for free.

At the node end, everything funnels through one switch. Node::_notification, L68 maps NOTIFICATION_PROCESS to a virtual script call at L100 — and if your script does not override _process, nothing was ever registered for it, so the cost is a sorted array scan, not a function call. Scene entry works the same way: Node::_propagate_ready, L323 walks children depth-first and only then fires NOTIFICATION_READY at L336, which is why parents are always ready before children fire. Groups are also the engine’s unit of threading: a node can set its process group to sub-thread, and _process_groups_thread, L1254 runs whole groups on worker threads while the main thread handles the rest.

Why Godot Calls Its Backends “Servers”

The server layer is the engine’s firewall between scene code and hardware state. When a Sprite2D changes position, it does not render anything; it updates an RID the renderer already knows about. Those updates accumulate in a command queue, and RenderingServerDefault::sync, L439 is the drain point. When threading is on, init, L276 spawns a pump task on the worker pool whose loop at L419 keeps flushing the queue, and draw, L447 merely pushes _draw onto that same queue — the main thread never touches the GPU API. The draw implementation then runs a fixed sequence: begin the rasterizer frame, update scene and canvas state (L96), draw viewports (L109), end the frame (L115).

The same pattern repeats for physics, and here the abstraction is load-bearing. PhysicsServer3D, L391 declares three pure-virtual methods every backend must implement, and a small manager picks the implementation from project settings at boot. The default solver ships as a module, and the Jolt integration registers itself as an alternative at register_types, L60 — swapping physics engines is a settings change, not a code change. This thin-scene-over-fat-backends design is the same instinct behind the Rust ecosystem’s /rust/ approach of keeping engine systems behind data-oriented boundaries; Godot just expresses the boundary as singletons and RIDs instead of traits.

GDScript: A Bytecode VM Living in the Engine

Loading a script runs a miniature compiler inside the engine. GDScript::reload, L737 drives the whole flow: it feeds the source to GDScriptParser::parse, L448, where a hand-written tokenizer at L482 streams tokens into a recursive-descent parser. The AST then goes through an analyzer that resolves types and flags invalid expressions, and finally through GDScriptCompiler::compile, L3283, which walks each class (L3016) and every expression (L255) while a byte-code generator emits opcodes into a GDScriptFunction. This is why typing a script in the editor feels instant — parsing and analysis run incrementally for diagnostics long before you press play.

Execution is a Variant-stack interpreter with a distinctive trick. GDScriptFunction::call, L465 allocates the stack, then dispatches each instruction through DISPATCH_OPCODE — on GCC and Clang this is a computed goto *switch_table_ops[...] at L394, the same threaded-code technique that keeps interpreter loops fast; MSVC falls back to a plain switch at L409. Everything on the stack is a Variant, engine values are called directly rather than boxed, and a thread-local depth counter at L477 turns infinite recursion into an error. Awaited functions serialize their stack into a state object and resume from a saved instruction pointer, so await works without OS threads. If you have read the interpreter loops behind /php-src/ or browsed how /node/ embeds V8 as a script host, the shape is familiar — Godot just fused the host and the guest into one binary.

From SCons Build to First Scene

Godot builds with SCons, and the entry point is a plain Python SConstruct at the repo root. The two options that matter most are declared there: platform (also -p, auto-detected from your host, at L161) and target, whose choices are editor, template_release, and template_debug with editor as the default (L164). So a local build is:

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/godotengine/godot.git
cd godot
scons platform=linux target=editor

The README defers platform specifics to the official compiling docs (README.md, L44), and scu_builders.py reveals a build optimization worth knowing: “single compilation unit” batches translate units per module to cut link times. Every feature module — GDScript, Jolt, Mono, WebRTC — plugs in through its own SCsub and register_types.cpp. Once the binary runs, Main::setup registers server types (L757) then scene types (L789), Main::start parses project.godot, instantiates your main scene under the tree root, and the ready propagation from the previous section fires — first scene alive.

Honest Limits

  • Master is 4.8.0 with status = "beta" in version.py; symbols and line numbers in this post will drift as development continues.
  • GDScript has no JIT: it is an opcode interpreter over Variants, with a computed-goto fast path on GCC/Clang only. The intended escape hatch for hot loops is moving them into C++ behind a server API — the engine’s own code does exactly that.
  • Two full 3D physics backends ship in-tree (godot_physics_3d, jolt_physics), selected by project settings through the manager; their behavior is not identical, and results differ between them.
  • The server split adds a one-frame latency shape: scene changes are queued, and only sync/draw make them visible, which matters when mixing direct server calls with node APIs.
  • The engine carries 59 module directories and a servers/ tree spanning 12 subsystems (audio, camera, debugger, display, movie_writer, navigation, physics, rendering, text, xr) — the source tour here covers the spine, not the skin.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Godot's master branch: how Main::iteration drives a frame, how the scene tree dispatches _process, why backends are called servers, and how GDScript compiles to bytecode.

entry.title: Inside LÖVE: How Lua Callbacks Drive the Simplest 2D Game Framework

link.title: Inside LÖVE: How Lua Callbacks Drive the Simplest 2D Game Framework

entry.content:
A complete LÖVE game fits in a single main.lua that is often shorter than this article. You define love.load(), love.update(dt), and love.draw(), run love, and a window opens with a running game. After configuring scenes and build settings in bigger engines before anything appears on screen, that economy feels almost suspicious. Something has to be doing the real work — so where is it?

The answer is stranger than tutorials admit: the “main loop” of a LÖVE game is itself Lua code. When your main.lua never defines love.run, the loop your game lives inside is boot.lua and callbacks.lua — two Lua scripts that are compiled into the native binary as C string literals, executed by a Lua state that the C++ main() creates and then serves as a coroutine host. Your callbacks are not hooking into C++; they are being called from another Lua script that C++ merely resumes.

And the .love file your game gets packaged into? It is an ordinary zip archive that the engine mounts as a virtual filesystem at boot, before your code has even loaded. This post walks the actual source of the love2d/love repository (the main branch, currently version 12.0, codename “Bestest Friend”) to show how each stage really works.

Overview: from the native executable, through the embedded Lua boot scripts, down to the SDL3 window, PhysFS filesystem, and renderer backends.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The executable’s main() is almost trivial: it checks version consistency, then runs runlove() in a do/while loop so the engine can restart the entire Lua state on demand — runlove, L168.
  • Inside, luaL_newstate() creates a stock Lua VM and luaL_openlibs opens the standard libraries — no engine-specific Lua fork involved, just luaL_newstate, L190.
  • luaopen_love in the love module preloads a big table of love.* module loaders plus the boot scripts, all driven from one static modules table, L182.
  • The boot scripts are not files on disk: boot.lua, callbacks.lua, arg.lua, and jitsetup.lua are #included as raw string literals at arg_lua, L90 and loaded with luaL_loadbuffer.
  • love.boot() finds the game source — the exe path itself for fused games — by attempting love.filesystem.setSource inside a pcall, see setSource call, L77.
  • love.init() builds a default config table, then lets your game’s conf.lua mutate it through love.conf(c) before any module is loaded — conf.lua loading, L249.
  • Only after config does it require the enabled modules in a fixed order and open the window with love.window.setMode — module require loop, L348.
  • The default love.run, L168 is a returned closure: pump events, dispatch them through the love.handlers table, step the timer, call love.update(dt), clear, call love.draw(), then present() — draw and present, L199.
  • Crashes never hit the OS dialog: love.errorhandler builds the famous blue error screen and returns its own event loop — errorhandler, L221.

Detail view: the boot chain from main() to main.lua, the CMake feature switches, and how each module wrapper reaches its native backend.

The Boot Script Is Compiled Into the Binary

LÖVE inverts the usual embedding story. Neovim loads its Lua files from disk at startup, and embedding a Python interpreter — as in our CPython source tour — means marshalling your own initialization sequence in C. LÖVE instead bakes its Lua scaffolding directly into the executable. In src/modules/love/love.cpp, four Lua files become static const char[] arrays via #include, so luaopen_love_boot just calls luaL_loadbuffer over an in-memory string — luaopen_love_boot, L813. There is no filesystem lookup that could fail or be tampered with; the boot process is literally part of the binary image.

The C++ side then drives the boot script as a coroutine. In src/love.cpp, after require "love.boot", the returned function is moved onto a new Lua thread and resumed in a loop until it stops yielding — luax_resume loop, L265. That yields-while-running structure is what lets the boot sequence suspend itself: love.boot() and love.init() run first, then the boot script hands control to whatever love.run returns, and the C++ loop keeps resuming that closure every frame until it returns an exit code. If the boot script returns the string "restart" instead, main() throws the whole Lua state away and calls runlove() again, which is how love.event.quit("restart") achieves a clean hot reset — restart value check, L280.

One more preload happens before arguments are even parsed: love.jitsetup. The script checks whether the jit table exists and silently returns if it does not, then tunes the JIT compiler with doubled trace limits — jit.opt.start, L30. It is a no-op on plain Lua builds, and its existence tells you LÖVE treats the Lua runtime as a swappable dependency rather than an identity.

love.run: The Loop Every Game Inherits

The event plumbing explains LÖVE’s whole programming model. love.createhandlers() builds a metatable-guarded table where each entry — keypressed, mousemoved, resize, dozens more — wraps the corresponding user callback in a nil check, and indexing an unknown event name raises immediately via __index — createhandlers, L27. The SDL backend’s Event::pump polls the native queue and converts each SDL_Event into a typed message — Event::pump, L127 — which the Lua loop iterates and dispatches by name. So love.keypressed in your game is three indirections deep: SDL callback data, a Lua message object, then the handler table.

The frame itself is five lines of policy. love.timer.step() computes dt from the previous frame, your love.update(dt) runs, then — only if love.graphics.isActive() — the loop resets the transform, clears with the background color, calls love.draw(), and presents. Timer::step in the timer module is where that dt comes from — Timer::step, L58. A 1 ms sleep keeps the loop from spinning the CPU when vsync is off — timer.sleep, L204. Nothing here is magic; every documented LÖVE behavior is one readable Lua function.

One Graphics API, Three Backends

The 12.x series restructured love.graphics into a backend-agnostic core with three implementations. The abstract Graphics::createInstance walks a static rendererOrder array and asks each compiled-in backend to create itself: vulkan::createInstance(), opengl::createInstance(), or metal::createInstance() — Graphics::createInstance, L165. The preference list is platform-shaped — Metal, Vulkan, OpenGL, with Metal first on Apple and Vulkan first elsewhere — defined in rendererOrder, L118. Games can override it from conf.lua via t.graphics.renderers, which love.init forwards into C++ before any window exists — renderer selection, L282.

Crucially, the window module and graphics module negotiate at creation time. Window::setWindow maps the chosen renderer to SDL window flags (SDL_WINDOW_OPENGL, SDL_WINDOW_METAL, SDL_WINDOW_VULKAN), calls createWindowAndContext, and then hands the native context to graphics->setMode — graphics->setMode, L673. For OpenGL that means SDL_GL_CreateContext on the fresh window — SDL_GL_CreateContext, L342 — followed by the GL backend’s own setMode, which queries the driver with glGetString(GL_VERSION) and initializes capabilities — opengl::Graphics::setMode, L285. The same love.graphics calls your game makes end up as command buffers on Metal, Vulkan submissions, or GL state changes, depending on which backend won the negotiation. If you have read our SDL article, you will recognize how much of the platform layer LÖVE simply delegates to SDL3 — CMake even pins the dependency at version 3.1.3 or newer — find_package(SDL3), L178.

From Makefile Build to First Window

The historical Makefile-based build is gone from the tree; the repository is now CMake-first, and the project’s readme is explicit that *nix in-tree builds are not allowed — you generate into a separate directory with cmake -B build -S . and cmake --build build --target install — per the official compilation instructions. On Windows the supported path is the separate megasource dependency repository, which vendors every library so MSVC users avoid DLL hunting. macOS builds go through the checked-in Xcode project at platform/xcode/love.xcodeproj with Apple frameworks supplied from the love-apple-dependencies repo, and platform/unix/debian/ carries the Debian packaging rules.

The dependency picture is visible in CMake itself: SDL3 3.1.3+, OpenAL, FreeType, and HarfBuzz, plus a LOVE_JIT option that controls the Lua runtime — option(LOVE_JIT), L91. The first window appears through the chain the diagram shows: love.init calls love.window.setMode with your conf table, w_setMode in the wrapper parses a WindowSettings struct and forwards to the SDL implementation — w_setMode, L130 — Window::setWindow creates the window and context — Window::setWindow, L471 — and only after the graphics backend accepts the context does love.init finally require your main.lua — require main.lua, L444. By the time your first line of game code runs, the window is open and a frame budget is already ticking. For a comparable “small framework, big surface” design, see also our raylib source tour — raylib makes the opposite trade, owning its windowing instead of delegating it.

The .love File Is Just a PhysFS Mount

Packaging a LÖVE game means zipping main.lua and friends into a .love archive, and the runtime treats it exactly that way. Filesystem::setSource in the PhysFS backend canonicalizes the path and calls PHYSFS_mount on it — PHYSFS_mount, L323. PhysFS abstracts directories and zip archives behind the same interface, so love.filesystem.read("main.lua") works identically whether the game is a folder or an archive. PhysFS searches the game source mount first, then the writable identity directory for saves.

Fused games — executables with a game appended — use a cleverer trick. If a plain PHYSFS_mount of the executable fails, the code builds a StripSuffixIo wrapper that scans the tail of the file to find where the appended zip begins, then mounts via PHYSFS_mountIo with that offset — StripSuffixIo, L330. That is how a single .exe contains both engine and game. The Lua surface is thin: w_setSource in the wrapper forwards one string argument — w_setSource, L97 — and love.boot’s fused detection at startup simply pcalls it against the exe path. Audio and physics slot into the same pattern: the OpenAL backend opens a device and context and spawns a dedicated mixer thread — PoolThread, L203 — while the Box2D world wrapper scales pixels down to meters and steps the simulation with the classic 8/3 velocity/position iterations — World::update, L307.

Honest Limits

The Lua runtime story has real wrinkles. LuaJIT is the default on Windows and Linux, but the build explicitly disables it on Apple platforms — LOVE_DEFAULT_JIT is false when CMake detects APPLE, with a “JIT not supported yet on Mac” warning — LOVE_DEFAULT_JIT, L85.
