Builds without LOVE_JIT link plain Lua instead, and the tree vendors a Lua 5.3 copy under src/libraries/lua53 used for the utf8 library preload. The source is candid about LuaJIT’s failure modes too: luaopen_love installs a lua_atpanic handler specifically because LuaJIT can abort on out-of-memory rather than raise, and the comment warns it is “not foolproof” — lua_atpanic, L676.

Two more caveats belong here. First, the main branch is the development line for the next major release — the readme states plainly it “should not be considered stable” — so line numbers cited here describe 12.0 development, and the 11.x series you probably have installed differs significantly (it has no Vulkan or Metal backends and uses LuaJIT everywhere). Second, the framework trusts the platform delegate for windowing and input, so LÖVE inherits SDL3’s behavior on obscure platforms rather than papering over it; the C++ main() even special-cases iOS to convert every quit into a restart because programmatic exit is disallowed there. None of this diminishes the design achievement: one readable Lua loop, a binary-baked boot chain, and clean seams where SDL3, PhysFS, OpenAL, and Box2D plug in.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of the LÖVE 2D game framework: the embedded boot.lua, the love.run callback loop, SDL3 windowing, OpenGL/Vulkan/Metal backends, OpenAL audio, Box2D physics, and PhysFS zip mounting.

entry.title: Inside MonoGame: The XNA Successor’s Game Loop, SpriteBatch, and Content Pipeline

link.title: Inside MonoGame: The XNA Successor’s Game Loop, SpriteBatch, and Content Pipeline

entry.content:
Stardew Valley, Celeste, Streets of Rage 4, and Carrion were all built on MonoGame — an open-source re-implementation of Microsoft’s discontinued XNA Framework. The deal XNA offered is seductive: you subclass Game, override Update and Draw, call base.Run(), and a window opens with your game running at 60 frames per second. The framework disappears. That is exactly the problem when something goes wrong — a frame hitch, an audio stutter, a load that takes twice as long on Android — and the answer lives seven hundred lines deep in a file you never wrote.

So what actually happens in one tick? The engine accumulates Stopwatch ticks since the last frame, runs as many fixed-length Update calls as the accumulator allows, then draws exactly once and presents the back buffer. And why does SpriteBatch exist as a concept at all? Because drawing 5,000 sprites as 5,000 individual GPU calls would drown the driver in state changes; instead every sprite becomes a pooled quad in a queue that gets sorted, sliced into 16-bit-index-sized chunks, and flushed as triangle lists. Neither behavior is magic — it is all in the tree.

This post walks the develop branch of the MonoGame repository file by file. The two diagrams below were generated from the actual repo tree, and every source link goes to the exact line cited. If you have read our tour of raylib, this is the heavier, class-shaped counterpart: an XNA-shaped framework rather than a flat C API.

Overview of MonoGame's architecture on the develop branch: the Game core talks to an abstract platform host, which on desktop is the SDL backend; SpriteBatch funnels quads through SpriteBatcher into GraphicsDevice, while Content, Input, and Audio hang off the same Game object.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The Game constructor does not just set fields — it builds a ContentManager, then asks GamePlatform.PlatformCreate(this) for a platform host and stores it in the Platform field (Game, L64, Game, L73).
  • PlatformCreate is a compile-time switch: desktop builds bound to DESKTOPGL or ANGLE get SdlGamePlatform; the Windows DirectX build gets WinFormsGamePlatform (GamePlatform.Desktop, L11).
  • Game.Run() delegates to the platform’s DefaultRunBehavior; the synchronous path calls one DoUpdate before the window even shows, then blocks in Platform.RunLoop() (Game, L454, Game, L486).
  • The SDL run loop is a plain while (true): poll SDL events, call Game.Tick(), run queued cross-thread callbacks, dispose stale GL contexts (SDLGamePlatform, L84).
  • Inside Tick, the fixed timestep sleeps in 1 ms slices until a full 60 fps slot has accumulated, then runs catch-up Update calls — and flags IsRunningSlowly once lag exceeds five frames (Game, L512, Game, L579).
  • SpriteBatch.End() is the flush point: it applies render state, then hands the whole queue to SpriteBatcher.DrawBatch (SpriteBatch, L115, SpriteBatch, L125).
  • The batcher sorts queued quads, flushes whenever the texture changes, and issues DrawUserIndexedPrimitives triangle lists capped at short.MaxValue / 6 quads per call (SpriteBatcher, L167, SpriteBatcher, L204).
  • ContentManager.Load<T> normalizes the asset name to a /-separated key, serves repeat loads from a dictionary cache, and opens the stream by appending .xnb (ContentManager, L341, ContentManager, L385).
  • Input and audio plug into the same event stream: SDL controller events feed GamePad, while FrameworkDispatcher.Update — called inside every DoUpdate — pumps the audio system (GamePad, L42, Game, L821).

The detail view expands each group: the GamePlatform family (SDL, WinForms, Web, Android), the SpriteBatch-to-GraphicsDevice flush path with its OpenGL and DirectX partials, the build-time tools behind XNB assets, and the OpenAL/XAudio audio split.

The Game Class: One Tick at a Time

Game is a partial class — a single logical object spread across one shared file plus per-platform partials. The constructor wires the essentials: a GameServiceContainer, a ContentManager registered against it, and the GamePlatform host (Game, L64). Two defaults matter more than people realize: _isFixedTimeStep = true and _targetElapsedTime = TimeSpan.FromTicks(166667) — 60 fps, written as a literal comment in the source (Game, L51).

The interesting code is Tick(). The word “sensitive” appears in a comment above it, and the comment is not joking. Each call first adds elapsed Stopwatch ticks to an accumulator (Game, L532). If fixed-step mode is on and less than one target slot has elapsed, the loop sleeps — Windows uses a precision timer helper, other platforms fall back to 1 ms sleeps — and jumps back to a RetryTick label rather than re-entering the method (Game, L536). That is why a MonoGame idle frame costs almost nothing on Windows.

Once a slot is ready, a while loop drains the accumulator in 60 fps increments, calling DoUpdate per step (Game, L561). This is the classic “catch-up” pattern: if a frame took 100 ms, you get six updates and still exactly one draw. Extra catch-up steps increment a frame-lag counter; five or more lagging frames flips IsRunningSlowly to true, which your code can observe through GameTime (Game, L579). Variable timestep mode is the degenerate case: one update, accumulator zeroed.

Both update and draw funnel through internal wrappers. DoUpdate consults Platform.BeforeUpdate (a hook platforms can use to veto), then calls FrameworkDispatcher.Update() before your override — that call is what keeps audio queues flowing without any action from you (Game, L816). DoDraw requires both Platform.BeforeDraw and BeginDraw to pass; afterward EndDraw calls Platform.Present(), handing the finished frame to the OS compositor (Game, L830, Game, L645).

The Platform Wall: GamePlatform and SDL

Everything OS-specific sits behind GamePlatform, L13, an abstract class whose contract is small but strict: a DefaultRunBehavior, RunLoop() that blocks until exit, and BeforeUpdate/BeforeDraw veto hooks (GamePlatform, L47, GamePlatform, L156). The desktop factory is four lines long: DESKTOPGL || ANGLE yields SdlGamePlatform, WINDOWS && DIRECTX yields the WinForms host (GamePlatform.Desktop, L14). That means the “DesktopGL” NuGet package and the mobile builds share the exact same SDL windowing path — the same library our SDL source tour covered from the C side.

SdlGamePlatform.RunLoop is refreshingly honest about what a game loop is. Each iteration drains SDL’s event queue through Sdl.PollEvent — quit events become Game.Exit(), controller hot-plugs rebuild device lists, key events translate scancodes into XNA Keys (SDLGamePlatform, L84, SDLGamePlatform, L120) — then calls Game.Tick(), pumps Threading.Run() (the queue that lets background threads schedule work onto the game thread), and disposes contexts the graphics device no longer needs. The window itself is an SdlGameWindow, created with a literal Sdl.Window.Create call (SDLGameWindow, L14, SDLGameWindow, L133).

How many platforms is this wall fronting? The MonoGamePlatform enum in Utilities enumerates fourteen: Android, iOS, tvOS, DesktopGL, Windows, WebGL, XboxOne, WindowsDX12, XboxSeries, PlayStation4, PlayStation5, NintendoSwitch, DesktopVK, and NintendoSwitch2 (MonoGamePlatform, L10). Each gets its own GamePlatform subclass; the SDL class is merely the one most desktop players ever touch.

SpriteBatch: Why 2D Games Don’t Talk to the GPU One Sprite at a Time

SpriteBatch looks like a convenience API, but it is really a performance contract. Its constructor builds two collaborators: a SpriteEffect (the built-in shader every sprite goes through) and a SpriteBatcher (the queue) with a capacity rounded up in chunks of 64 (SpriteBatch, L49).

Begin records render state — blend, sampler, depth, rasterizer, an optional transform — and by default defers all GPU work to End; if you pass SpriteSortMode.Immediate, it flips the model and applies state right away (SpriteBatch, L79). Every Draw call between the two does almost nothing: it leases a pooled SpriteBatchItem from the batcher, computes a SortKey depending on the sort mode (texture sorting for draw-call coalescing, layer depth for front-to-back), and writes texture coordinates into the quad (SpriteBatch, L179, SpriteBatch, L195). Rotation-zero sprites even take a hand-inlined fast path that skips the matrix math.

End is where the queue becomes triangles (SpriteBatch, L115). DrawBatch sorts eligible modes with a plain Array.Sort, then walks the items in chunks of short.MaxValue / 6 — 5,461 quads, because the index buffer is 16-bit (SpriteBatcher, L30). The inner loop keeps a “current texture” pointer; the moment the next item’s texture differs, it flushes what it has and rebinds (SpriteBatcher, L204). That is the real reason texture atlases matter in MonoGame: fewer texture changes means fewer flushes, and fewer flushes means fewer draw calls.

The flush itself, FlushVertexArray, copies quad vertices into a flat array and calls DrawUserIndexedPrimitives with a TriangleList, passing (vertexCount / 4) * 2 triangles (SpriteBatcher, L242, SpriteBatcher, L261). GraphicsDevice.Present then closes the frame — it refuses to run while a render target is bound, resets the metrics counters, and delegates to the platform partial (GraphicsDevice, L741). The same device object carries OpenGL and DirectX implementation partials behind partial methods, which is how one API spans both backends (GraphicsDevice, L748).

From dotnet Build to First Window

Everything above is buildable from source in a few commands, straight from the repo’s own instructions. Clone with submodules — the native libraries are submodules, not subdirectories — then initialize them: git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/MonoGame/MonoGame.git followed by git submodule update --init (README, L103). There is no root-wide solution to open; instead the repo ships per-target solutions (MonoGame.Framework.DesktopGL.sln, MonoGame.Framework.WindowsDX.sln, a native console solution) plus separate tool solutions per OS (README, L105). The DesktopGL project targets net8.0 (DesktopGL.csproj, L4), so any modern dotnet build restores and compiles it, and build.ps1/build.sh at the root wrap the full matrix.

The build-time side of content lives in its own project. ContentBuilder is the abstract entry point: a queue of content requests, parameters from CLI args, and a BuildAndWriteContent method that processes one asset and writes the compiled result (ContentBuilder, L17, ContentBuilder, L79). Three tools front it: mgcb for the command line, mgcb-editor as a GUI, and mgfxc for compiling effects (README, L115). With the framework built, the first window is a dozen lines: subclass Game, override Initialize/Update/Draw, call Run(). The host chain does the rest — PlatformCreate constructs the SDL host, whose constructor immediately creates the SdlGameWindow (SDLGamePlatform, L61); DoInitialize creates the actual device through the GraphicsDeviceManager before your Initialize override runs (Game, L843); and the first Tick blocks in the sleep-accumulator until frame one is due.

Honest Limits

  • Console support is real but gated: the README lists PlayStation 4/5, Xbox, and Switch 1/2, all explicitly “for registered developers” — you cannot clone your way onto a Switch (README, L39).
  • Vulkan and DirectX 12 are marked preview for 3.8.5 in the README (README, L46); the enum carries DesktopVK and WindowsDX12 entries, but the shipping desktop backends remain OpenGL and DirectX 11.
  • The desktop factory covers exactly two paths — SDL and WinForms (GamePlatform.Desktop, L11). Mobile, web, and console hosts are separate partials, so a “platform” is a compile target, not a runtime setting.
  • The batcher’s doc comment promises support for int.MaxValue sprites but processes them in short.MaxValue vertex groups (SpriteBatcher, L11) — a hard 16-bit index ceiling per draw call, not an implementation detail you can tune.
  • The in-repo Templates folder contains the Visual Studio extension project (MonoGame.Templates.VSExtension); the C# starter templates themselves ship separately via NuGet (README, L112, README, L127).
  • The new ContentBuilder console framework is labeled preview by the README (README, L118), and the class is abstract — the stabilized build path is the mgcb tool.
  • MonoGame is deliberately engine-less: no editor, no scene graph, no physics. If you want those prebuilt, that is a reason to look at Godot instead; if you want the same SDL-plus-simplicity philosophy in Lua, LÖVE is the closest cousin.
entry.summary: How MonoGame actually runs a game: Game.Tick fixed timestep, GamePlatform SDL hosts, SpriteBatch quad batching, and the XNB content build system, traced through source.

entry.title: Inside Phaser: The Scene Lifecycle and Step Loop Behind 2D Web Games

link.title: Inside Phaser: The Scene Lifecycle and Step Loop Behind 2D Web Games

entry.content:
A Phaser game ships as one JavaScript bundle and then runs on a five-year-old Android phone, a school Chromebook, and a desktop browser at 144 Hz. That is a strange engineering target for a game engine: no install step, no runtime download, and a memory budget smaller than a single Unity texture atlas. Most engine projects solve this by being small at the core, and Phaser’s answer is visible immediately in its dependency list — the entire runtime depends on exactly one package, an event emitter. Everything else you think of as “the engine” is plain code in one tree that you can read in an afternoon.

So what actually happens in one tick? A browser callback fires, Phaser computes a clamped delta value, runs your scene’s update, steps every physics body, sorts the display list by depth, walks each camera, and flushes the GPU or 2D-context commands — then throws it all away and does it again next frame. The order is not incidental. It is a fixed sequence of events written into a single ~50-line method, and once you see it, every Phaser bug you have met (“my physics are one frame behind”, “my sprite flickers behind the UI”) becomes readable in terms of which stage of the tick ran first.

The other organizing idea is the Scene. If you come from a native engine like Godot, a Phaser Scene is closest to a tree node plus its own update loop, but Phaser generalizes it: every screen, menu, and overlay is a Scene with the same lifecycle — init, preload, create, update — and the engine itself is just a scheduler that steps scenes in one order and renders them in another. This post walks that whole loop through the actual source of the phaserjs/phaser repository, from boot to first pixel.

Overview of the Phaser architecture as built by Game.boot: the TimeStep loop drives Game.step, which fans out to the SceneManager, the renderers, and the manager plugins that hang off each scene's Systems bundle.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Boot is event-gated. Game.boot, L350 creates the renderer, the DOM container, and the canvas, but the game loop does not start here — it waits for the Texture Manager to emit READY, then calls start.
  • The renderer is chosen once, at boot. CreateRenderer, L44 resolves the default renderType with Features.webGL ? CONST.WEBGL : CONST.CANVAS and throws if the explicitly requested context cannot be created.
  • TimeStep.step, L718 is where the browser hands control over: it clamps negative deltas (a Chrome quirk), optionally smooths the delta to kill frame-time spikes, and only then calls the Game callback.
  • Game.step, L454 is the frame contract: PRE_STEP, user STEP, scene update, POST_STEP, renderer preRender, scene render, postRender — always in that order, every frame.
  • Scenes update in reverse list order and render in forward list order. SceneManager.update, L558 walks the array backwards so an overlay launched later steps after (and can freeze) the scene beneath it.
  • A scene is a status machine, not just a class: bootScene, L473 calls init, resets the loader, runs preload, and only flips the status to RUNNING after create finishes.
  • Rendering is not incremental. Systems.render, L374 depth-sorts the display list and hands it to the cameras on every single frame.
  • Physics and input are not special-cased in the loop — they are scene plugins that subscribe to the same events. ArcadePhysics.start, L130 wires the World to the scene’s UPDATE and POST_UPDATE events and nothing more.

The detail view follows one tick through the call graph: from the TimeStep tick, through Game.step, into the scene status machine, the display list sort, both renderer implementations, the arcade World step, and the input dispatch path.

One Tick: PreStep, Update, Render

The loop begins in Game.start, which binds Game.step into the TimeStep’s animation-frame runner. Each browser tick, TimeStep.step, L718 computes Math.max(0, time - lastTime) — the clamp matters because browsers occasionally report negative deltas — and passes the result through a smoothing step before invoking the callback. This is the only place Phaser cares about real wall-clock time; everything downstream works in the smoothed delta it is handed.

Game.step then emits its event sequence. The interesting decision is what lives where. Global managers like Input and Sound update on PRE_STEP, before any scene logic, so a pointer position is fresh for the frame. Your own game.events handlers get STEP, and only after that does the SceneManager receive update(time, delta). Rendering is deliberately outside the update phase: renderer.preRender clears buffers and applies background colors, then scene.render walks scenes, then postRender handles snapshots. If you have ever written a postrender handler and wondered why the canvas is already “final”, this order is why.

Scenes: Boot, Preload, Create, Update

A Scene instance itself is nearly empty — its constructor just builds a Systems bundle and stores it as this.sys. Everything you actually use in a scene class (add, load, cameras, input, physics, tweens) is a plugin injected into that bundle at init time. That is why the API surface feels huge while the Scene class stays tiny: the class is a namespace, the plugin registry is the engine.

The lifecycle lives in the SceneManager. bootScene, L473 calls scene.init if it exists, resets the loader, and branches: if the scene defines preload, the loader is started and the scene waits; otherwise it jumps straight to create. On loader completion, create runs, the scene’s own update method is bound as the step hook, and the status finally becomes RUNNING — the gate checked by the update loop. Queued scenes are drained by processQueue at the top of every frame, which is how scene.start and scene.launch stay safe to call from inside a running scene.

The update/render asymmetry is the detail most Phaser developers eventually meet. Updates run in reverse list order so that scenes launched later step first — an overlay UI updates before the paused world under it. Rendering runs in forward order so that base scenes paint first and overlays composite on top. Nothing enforces this beyond the two loop directions; it is a pure index-ordering trick that substitutes for a layer system.

Game Objects, Depth Sort, and Two Renderers

Every visible thing is a Game Object registered in the scene’s DisplayList, a typed wrapper over an array. There is no scene graph to traverse by default: draw order is literally list order, and the depth value you set on a sprite is a sort key, not a tree position. Each frame, Systems.render, L374 calls displayList.depthSort() before any drawing happens, so changing a depth mid-update takes effect the same frame — but the sort is a full pass over the list, which is one reason deep scenes get expensive.

Position data follows the same “compute on demand” philosophy. A sprite’s transform component stores x, y, rotation, and scale, and Transform, L494 composes those into a matrix via applyITRS only when something asks for it. Nested containers multiply that through a parent matrix, which is how transforms accumulate without per-object matrix caching.

The two renderers implement the same contract — preRender, render per camera, postRender — from boot time. The WebGL side batches sprite draws into GPU calls and routes each camera’s visible children through render nodes; if you have read how three.js organizes its scene graph for GPU submission, the camera-to-renderer handoff will look familiar, just with 2D batching instead of mesh trees. The Canvas fallback is an immediate-mode 2D-context implementation of the identical interface, which is what lets the same game code run on devices without WebGL support.

From npm Install to First Scene

The repository is a plain Node-style package, and Node tooling is all it needs. package.json declares exactly one runtime dependency (eventemitter3) and builds with webpack: npm run build runs webpack --config config/webpack.config.js, a separate dist script produces the minified release bundle, and npm test runs vitest. The published main entry points at src/phaser.js while the browser field points at the webpack-built dist/phaser.js, so consuming the source directly and the bundle behave differently by design.

TypeScript support is generated rather than hand-maintained: the tsgen script runs jsdoc over the source tree and emits types/phaser.d.ts, then compiles a test project against those types. Unlike reading a compiler that is written in its own language, such as the TypeScript source, the JSDoc comments here are not optional flavor — the same comments are the shipped API documentation and the type surface.

Your first scene, from the engine’s perspective: the config’s scene array is passed to the SceneManager constructor, which immediately queues the class; the first update drains the queue, boots the scene, runs its init and preload, waits for the loader, calls create, and marks it RUNNING. From then on your update(time, delta) is called once per tick until the scene is stopped or sleeps.

Physics and Input: Just Scene Events

The clearest architectural statement in the codebase is that physics does not appear anywhere in Game.step. Instead, ArcadePhysics.start, L130 subscribes the World to the scene’s UPDATE event, and the World maintains its own fixed-step accumulator: it integrates velocity into position only when accumulated elapsed time crosses the frame budget, which keeps simulation speed independent of render rate. The step itself (World.step, L1019) updates every enabled body, reloads the collision tree, and runs the active collider pairs — in that order, so collisions resolve against freshly integrated positions.

The Body-object dance explains the classic “one frame behind” feeling. Each frame, the UpdateList calls preUpdate on registered sprites, and Body.preUpdate, L1127 first syncs the body to wherever its GameObject was placed, then integrates. After collision resolution, the body writes positions back to the GameObjects during POST_UPDATE. Reading input positions happens even earlier, in the PRE_STEP phase handled by the global InputManager, which captures DOM events once and forwards them to per-scene InputPlugins for hit testing.

Honest Limits

The tree is Phaser 4 — package.json reports version 4.2.1 (release “Giedi”) — and Phaser 4’s structure is visible in the source: renderer-side effects live under src/filters and operate on WebGL texture wrappers, so the Canvas fallback path cannot run them; that split is inherent to the two-renderer design, not a missing feature. The CanvasRenderer also describes itself with batching methods that end in immediate 2D-context calls, so performance parity with WebGL is not the goal.

Two more limits worth naming. First, the “engine” is a plugin registry assembled at scene init, which makes the API surface discoverable only through the generated type definitions and JSDoc — the source comments are the documentation, and there is no separate spec to check them against. Second, the fixed-step physics accumulator applies to the arcade World; other scene plugins are driven purely by the frame delta, so mixing subsystems means mixing time models. None of this is hidden — it is all readable in the four files this post linked to — but it is the kind of thing you only learn by reading the source, which is exactly the point of walking it.
entry.summary: How the Phaser source runs a 2D web game: the TimeStep loop, SceneManager lifecycle, depth sorting, arcade physics integration, and the WebGL and Canvas renderers.

entry.title: Inside PixiJS: How the Batcher Turns Thousands of Sprites into One Draw Call

link.title: Inside PixiJS: How the Batcher Turns Thousands of Sprites into One Draw Call

entry.content:
Thousands of moving sprites are where naive canvas-2D code goes to die. A loop of drawImage calls crosses the JavaScript-to-native boundary thousands of times per frame, re-sends state on every call, and gives the GPU nothing it can chew on in parallel. Particle fields, tile maps, and bullet-hell wave patterns all hit that wall somewhere between a couple thousand images and whatever fps you promised your designer. PixiJS draws the same workload at 60 fps, and the reason is unglamorous: it almost never draws things one at a time. Sprites that share state get merged into shared geometry buffers and submitted as a single draw call, so the GPU sees one object where your code sees ten thousand.

To find where that merging happens, follow one tick. PixiJS’s Ticker wraps requestAnimationFrame, and once per frame it walks a chained listener list. The Application’s TickerPlugin registers a low-priority listener that calls renderer.render(stage), which raises five runners, forces the stage into a render group, and lets per-type “pipes” flatten the tree into an instruction list. The batch pipe then packs every quad-shaped element into shared attribute and index buffers, and the backend — WebGL by default, WebGPU on request — uploads and executes them. Every stage in that chain exists to make the next stage’s work trivial.

This design is also why v8 was a rewrite rather than a patch. The renderer layer was rebuilt so that one scene graph, one set of pipes, and one batcher could talk to either a WebGL or a WebGPU device, with the backend picked at startup and loaded through a dynamic import so unused backends never enter your bundle. The diagrams below were generated from the actual source tree on the dev branch; the first shows the high-level loop, the second zooms into the batcher and both backends.

PixiJS v8 at a glance: the frame loop (left) drives the scene graph, which is flattened by pipes into batches executed by the selected renderer backend.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts with Ticker, L71. Its update method at L643 computes the frame delta, clamps it with minFPS/maxFPS, and walks the listener chain in a plain linked-list loop — no event dispatch, no allocations.
  • The Application bootstrap is thin. Application, L168 mostly forwards options, and its init at L254 simply awaits autoDetectRenderer; frame scheduling comes from the TickerPlugin, which adds itself at UPDATE_PRIORITY.LOW so user logic always runs before rendering.
  • Backend selection happens once, at startup. renderPriority, L42 in autoDetectRenderer.ts is literally ['webgl', 'webgpu', 'canvas'] — WebGL first — and the chosen backend is pulled in with a dynamic import, L127.
  • Container, L655 is the display-tree base: a children array plus dirty flags like didChange. Positioning a sprite flips a flag; nothing recomputes until the frame actually renders.
  • RenderGroupSystem, L25 is the heart of the walk: its render at L44 validates renderables, updates transforms, rebuilds instructions only when structure changed, then uploads and executes.
  • Sprites never draw themselves. SpritePipe.addRenderable, L29 wraps each sprite’s data into a BatchableSprite, L15 — 4 attributes, 6 indices, packAsQuad: true — and hands it to the batch pipe.
  • Batcher, L297 accumulates elements into one growing ViewableBuffer; Batcher.add, L430 just records index and attribute offsets for each element.
  • Assets stay out of the hot loop entirely. Assets.load, L573 resolves aliases against a cache first, so Sprite.from('bunny') after load is a dictionary hit, not an I/O.

The detail view: how sprites flow through SpritePipe into BatcherPipe, how DefaultBatcher packs quads, and which systems are shared versus backend-specific.

One Ticker Tick, Start to Finish

The ticker is deliberately boring, which is exactly what you want from a 60 Hz heartbeat. The _tick closure at L273 clears the pending animation-frame id, invokes update, and only re-arms requestAnimationFrame if listeners still exist — an empty ticker stops asking the browser for frames. Inside Ticker.update, L643, the raw elapsed time is stored separately from the capped delta, elapsedMS is clamped by _maxElapsedMS (your maxFPS setting) and scaled by speed, and a minFPS floor prevents huge deltas from teleporting your physics after a tab switch. Listeners are then emitted by walking the TickerListener chain directly, and the FPS getter, L733 derives its number from those raw measurements. Two singleton instances — Ticker.shared, L880 and Ticker.system — keep visual and internal bookkeeping on separate clocks, which is why background loading does not stutter your animation. The design also rewards restraint: the ticker only measures time and schedules callbacks, so a listener that finishes in a microsecond costs exactly as much as the slot it occupies — every expensive decision in PixiJS deliberately belongs to the render stage downstream, where it can be batched, pooled, or skipped.

From npm Install to First Sprite

Runtime install is two steps: npm install pixi.js, then:

import { Application, Assets, Sprite } from 'pixi.js';

const app = new Application();
await app.init({ preference: 'webgpu' }); // or leave the default
await Assets.load('assets/bunny.png');
app.stage.addChild(Sprite.from('bunny'));

app.init resolves the renderer through autoDetectRenderer, and Assets.load runs the resolver/parser/cache machinery visible in the assets group of the diagram — loadBundle, L753 does the same for named groups of assets, which is how games preload a level in one await.

If you want to build PixiJS itself, clone pixijs/pixijs and check package.json. The build runs through Node scripts (npm run build executes node ./scripts/build.mts), with build:lib producing the library variant in dev mode. Development iteration uses watch:lib, a nodemon process that rebuilds whenever src/** changes (-e ts,js,vert,frag,wgsl,d.ts — note the shader extensions; vertex, fragment, and WGSL files are first-class build inputs). Testing is also script-driven: test delegates to scripts/test.mts, with test:unit, test:visual (screenshot comparison), test:types, test:dts, and test:lint as targeted entry points. That is a typical modern TypeScript setup — if you enjoy reading language internals, the TypeScript source itself is a similar rabbit hole, and the tooling all runs on Node.

The Scene Graph Is Not the Draw List

The most important architectural fact in PixiJS is that the thing you manipulate and the thing the GPU consumes are two different data structures. Your Container tree (children at L717) is a mutable scene graph optimized for authoring. At render time, subtrees are attached to RenderGroups, each of which owns an InstructionSet, L17 — a flat, reusable array of instructions.

RenderGroupSystem._updateRenderGroups, L170 runs three phases. Phase one validates renderables (for sprites, validateRenderable, L48 asks whether the texture still fits in its current batch — if not, the batch must be rebuilt). Phase two updates transforms, but only for containers whose didChange flag was set since the last frame, tracked with a per-frame tick so nothing updates twice. Phase three is the interesting split: if the tree structure changed — children added, removed, reordered — _buildInstructions at L245 rebuilds the whole instruction list; otherwise it only re-packs the few elements in childrenRenderablesToUpdate. A static scene of ten thousand sprites therefore costs almost nothing to “render” at the CPU level: the list survives frame to frame, and execution just replays it. Mutating a parent transform stays cheap for the same reason — the group’s matrix changes once and children inherit it, without any instruction being rewritten.

Inside the Batcher: Six Floats per Vertex

Now the payoff. A sprite quad contributes exactly 4 vertices and 6 indices (BatchableSprite, L21). DefaultBatcher, L65 declares vertexSize = 6 at L81: for each vertex, two floats of screen-space position, two floats of UV, one packed uint32 ARGB color, and one packed uint32 holding the texture slot id and the round-pixels flag. packQuadAttributes, L152 transforms the four corners with the sprite’s world matrix (a 2×2 plus translation — pure arithmetic on a Float32Array) and writes the textureIdAndRound word as (textureId << 16) | roundPixels.

The batch pipe (BatcherPipe, L29) owns one active batcher at a time. addToBatch at L91 breaks the batch when the element’s batcher name differs — custom geometry goes through a different batcher — and batchers are created with maxTextures taken from renderer.limits.maxBatchableTextures. Where does that number come from? On WebGL, getMaxTexturesPerBatch, L14 probes MAX_TEXTURE_IMAGE_UNITS and then binary-searches how many if-statements the fragment shader can actually carry; on WebGPU, GpuLimitsSystem, L55 takes min(maxSampledTexturesPerShaderStage, maxSamplersPerShaderStage) straight from the device.

When a batch must split — different blend mode, different topology, or no free texture slot — Batcher.break, L484 flushes the accumulated range as a Batch instruction (pooled objects, so breaking is allocation-free at steady state) and starts the next one. At the end of the walk, buildEnd, L117 points the shared BatchGeometry buffers at the batch data, upload, L134 marks only dirty buffer ranges, and execute, L152 delegates to the backend adaptor. One drawElements call per batch; thousands of sprites per call.

One Scene Graph, Two GPU Backends

Because batching produces plain buffers and instruction objects, the backend is just an execution strategy. Both WebGLRenderer, L163 and WebGPURenderer, L158 extend AbstractRenderer, L204, whose render at L345 forces the stage into a render group and fires the prerender/renderStart/render/renderEnd/postrender runners. Runners (SystemRunner, L44) call same-named methods on every registered system, so a renderer is assembled from dozens of small systems — view, background, state, texture, geometry, batch — each tagged with the backends it supports.

Backend-specific work is isolated in adaptors: the batch pipe talks to GlBatchAdaptor or GpuBatchAdaptor, and WebGPU-only concepts live in the gpu/ tree — GpuDeviceSystem owns the device, BindGroupSystem caches bind groups for texture batches, and a PSO cache keys compiled shader-state objects so identical sprites reuse them. Shared services stay backend-neutral: TexturePool, L75 recycles render textures by size bucket through getOptimalTexture, L211, and global uniforms upload the world matrix once per frame. If you know three-js, the split feels familiar — there too, one scene graph feeds multiple renderer backends — and the same “many objects, few draw calls” math is why Phaser-class 2D game frameworks build their rendering on top of this kind of batcher.

Honest Limits

  • WebGL is still the default, not WebGPU. The code says so itself: autoDetectRenderer’s doc comment at L47 explains WebGL is prioritized “as it is the most tested safe API,” with WebGPU to be prioritized “in the near future.” You must pass preference: 'webgpu' (verified against isWebGPUSupported) to opt in.
  • A bad preference array can throw. If you restrict preference to backends the browser cannot provide, autoDetectRenderer raises No available renderer for the current environment at L167 — there is no silent last-resort beyond your list.
  • Batches are not free. Every blend-mode change, topology change, or texture-slot overflow splits the batch into another draw call. Heavy scenes mixing many blend modes and textures still pay per-batch overhead; the batcher’s own comment calls this out at L479.
  • v8 is a breaking change from v7. Custom shaders migrate through a helper (migrateFragmentFromV7toV8.ts exists for GL fragment code), and long-lived APIs are deprecated in-tree: Container.mixin since 8.8.0, TexturePool.textureStyle since 8.21.0, and the second argument of renderer.render since 8.0.0. Upgrading means reading the deprecation notes, not just the changelog.
  • The batcher contract tightened. Since v8.8.0, constructing a Batcher without an explicit maxTextures triggers a deprecation warning at L397 — batch capacity is now per-renderer configuration, not a global guess.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of PixiJS v8: how the Ticker, scene graph, render pipes, and sprite batcher turn thousands of sprites into a handful of draw calls on WebGL and WebGPU.
